content: Entecavir, when co-administered with metformin, may increase the risk of lactic acidosis. This interaction necessitates caution and close monitoring of the patient. When entecavir is co-administered with drugs such as moexipril, neomycin (oral), olmesartan, oxaliplatin, pamidronate, pemetrexed, pentamidine, perindopril, pindolol, plazomicin, polymyxin B, procainamide, quinapril, ramipril, risedronate, sacubitril/valsartan, streptomycin, sulindac, tacrolimus, telavancin, telmisartan, tobramycin (both systemic and inhaled), trandolapril, triamterene, valganciclovir, valsartan, zoledronic acid, or zonisamide, there is a potential for either drug to increase the effects of the other by reducing renal clearance. The clinical significance of these interactions is generally unknown, but caution is advised. Co-administration with drugs that impair renal function or compete for active tubular secretion may elevate serum concentrations of either entecavir or the co-administered drug. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) increases entecavir levels by reducing renal clearance, which may heighten the risk of toxicity. Both drugs are excreted via active tubular secretion, and their combined use requires careful monitoring. Common side effects of entecavir include fatigue (1-3%), headache (2-4%), dizziness, nausea, diarrhea, dyspepsia, vomiting, somnolence, and insomnia. Rare but serious adverse effects include lactic acidosis, increased transaminase levels, and severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis following drug discontinuation. Patients should be closely monitored for hepatic function after stopping therapy. Resistance to HIV nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) may develop in patients with unrecognized or untreated HIV infection. Entecavir is not recommended for patients co-infected with HIV and hepatitis B unless they are receiving highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported. Hypersensitivity reactions may occur. Caution is advised in patients with liver transplants or renal impairment. Discontinuation of anti-hepatitis therapy may lead to severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B, necessitating close monitoring of hepatic function for several months post-therapy. If appropriate, re-initiation of anti-hepatitis B therapy may be warranted. Pregnant women exposed to entecavir should be registered in the pregnancy registry by calling 1-800-258-4263. Data on the use of entecavir during pregnancy are insufficient to assess the risk of birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. It is unknown whether entecavir is present in human breast milk, affects milk production, or impacts the breastfed infant. In lactating rats, entecavir has been detected in milk. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for therapy and potential adverse effects on the infant. Entecavir is extensively distributed in tissues, with 13% protein binding. It is not a substrate, inducer, or inhibitor of the cytochrome P450 system. The drug is primarily excreted via the urine. Entecavir is used to treat chronic hepatitis B infection, which can lead to liver damage, liver cancer, and liver failure. It reduces the amount of hepatitis B virus in the body but is not a cure for hepatitis B. It is unknown if entecavir reduces the risk of liver cancer or liver damage. Patients should take entecavir exactly as prescribed, at evenly spaced intervals, and should not stop the medication without consulting their doctor. Stopping the drug may increase the viral load, make the infection harder to treat, or worsen side effects. Side effects such as headache, fatigue, dizziness, or nausea may occur. Serious allergic reactions are rare. Patients should seek medical advice for any side effects. Before taking entecavir, patients should inform their doctor of any allergies or other medical conditions. The drug may cause dizziness, and alcohol or marijuana use can exacerbate this effect. Patients should avoid driving or operating machinery until they are alert.
